note.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds between carbon atoms. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. To name a branched alkane, find the longest carbon chain, number it from the end nearest the branch, then give the branch its prefix and position number.
note.simple: Alkanes have only single bonds. Their names tell you the length of the main carbon chain and the names and positions of any branches.
note.checkQuestion: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃?
note.title: Alkanes and their names
steps: Find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Number the chain from the end closest to a branch.
Name each branch and give its position number.
Use the root for the longest chain and add the suffix -ane.
note.answer: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only carbon–carbon and carbon–hydrogen single bonds; their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

rationales: Alkanes do not have carbon–carbon multiple bonds, so this description is incorrect.
All four valencies of each carbon are used in single bonds to carbon or hydrogen.

written.text: Explain IUPAC system of nomenclature for alkanes.
written.finalAnswer: The root tells the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain, the suffix -ane identifies an alkane, and the prefix names any branch or branches. Number the chain from the end closest to a branch and give the branch its position number.

rubric.why: The root is selected from the longest continuous chain.
rubric.description: Explain what the root tells us.
rubric.how: State that the root tells the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.

rubric.why: The suffix identifies the class of compound.
rubric.description: Give the alkane suffix.
rubric.how: State that -ane is added for an alkane.

rubric.why: A prefix identifies groups attached to the parent chain.
rubric.description: Explain the role of the prefix.
rubric.how: State that the prefix tells the group or groups attached to the longest chain.

rubric.why: Numbering from the nearer end gives a branch its lowest possible locant.
rubric.description: Explain how to number the parent chain.
rubric.how: Number from the end closest to the branch.

rubric.why: The number and branch name are needed to make the complete name specific.
rubric.description: Show how a branch is named and located.
rubric.how: Give the branch name with its position number, such as 2-methylbutane.

modelAnswer: The root tells us the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain present in the molecule.
The suffix is added after the root and tells us about the class of organic compounds; for an alkane, the suffix is -ane.
The prefix is indicated before the root and tells us about the group or groups attached to the longest chain.
Number the longest continuous chain starting from the end closest to the branch.
Attach this number to the prefix to specify where the branch occurs.

written.text: Name the following compounds according to IUPAC system of nomenclature. (i) CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃ (ii) CH₃—C(CH₃)₂—CH₂—CH₃

rubric.why: The first structure requires the five-carbon parent chain and two correctly numbered methyl branches.
rubric.description: Name structure (i).
rubric.how: Identify pentane as the parent and place methyl branches at carbons 2 and 3.

rubric.why: The second structure requires the four-carbon parent chain and two methyl branches on carbon 2.
rubric.description: Name structure (ii).
rubric.how: Identify butane as the parent and place both methyl branches at carbon 2.

modelAnswer: (i) The longest chain has five carbon atoms; the methyl branches are at carbons 2 and 3.
The name is 2,3-dimethylpentane.
(ii) The longest chain has four carbon atoms; both methyl branches are at carbon 2.
The name is 2,2-dimethylbutane.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask for the general formula, the meaning of saturated, or an IUPAC name. State the formula or definition clearly and show the branch position in a name.
For nomenclature questions, marks can be earned for finding the longest chain, choosing the correct root and -ane suffix, numbering from the nearest end, and naming and locating each branch.
For questions comparing isomers, name both compounds and state the comparison directly; add a structural reason if the question asks how or why.
In structural-formula questions, check that the total carbon and hydrogen atoms agree with CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

explain.title: What makes an alkane?
explain.body: Alkanes are the simplest family of hydrocarbons with only carbon – carbon and carbon – hydrogen single bond. Alkanes are also called saturated hydrocarbons because all the four valencies of carbon in them are fully utilized either by hydrogen atoms or by other carbon atoms. Their general formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, where n is an integer.

explain.title: The parts of an IUPAC name
explain.body: Root: It tells us the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain present in the molecule. Suffix: It is added after the root and tells us about the class of organic compounds. Prefix: It is indicated before the root and tells us about the group or groups attached to the longest chain. For an alkane, the suffix is -ane.

explain.title: Roots to remember
explain.body: Meth- means 1 carbon, eth- 2, prop- 3, but- 4, pent- 5, hex- 6, hept- 7, oct- 8, non- 9 and dec- 10. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and is also called the parent hydrocarbon.

explain.title: How to name a branched alkane
explain.body: Choose the longest continuous chain. Number it from the end closest to a branch, name the branch as a prefix, and attach its position number. For example, the four-carbon chain in CH₃—CH(CH₃)—CH₂—CH₃ gives the name 2-methylbutane.

explain.title: Alkane structures
explain.body: A methyl group is CH₃ and a methylene group is CH₂. In a straight-chain alkane, the end carbon atoms are usually CH₃ groups, while the carbon atoms in the middle are CH₂ groups.

mistakes: Do not choose a shorter chain just because it looks like the main horizontal line; find the longest continuous carbon chain.
Do not number from the end farther from the branch; use the nearest end to give the lowest possible branch number.
Do not forget the locant (position number) before a branch name, such as 2-methylbutane.
Do not use an alkene suffix such as -ene for an alkane; alkanes take the suffix -ane.
Do not confuse a methyl group, CH₃, with a methylene group, CH₂.
